nodes.location: Back of the neck and the upper and middle back, from the base of the skull and the spine out to the collarbone and the shoulder blade.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves and steadies the shoulder blade. Its upper part raises it, its middle part pulls it back toward the spine, its lower part pulls it down, and the upper and lower parts turn it upward. The upper part also helps move the head and neck.
nodes.shapeNote: Together its three parts may contribute to the slope between the neck and the shoulder and to much of the surface of the upper back. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.

actions.label: Horizontal abduction

actions.note: Same wording as the shoulders lane's dossier. No own back muscle has a row for it in this dossier; the back lists it for its external member, the posterior deltoid.

actions.label: Elevation of the shoulder blade
actions.plainDescription: Raises the shoulder blade toward the ear, as in a shrug.

actions.label: Retraction of the shoulder blade
actions.plainDescription: Pulls the shoulder blade back toward the spine, drawing the shoulder blades together.

actions.label: Depression of the shoulder blade
actions.plainDescription: Pulls the shoulder blade down, away from the ear.
actions.note: Shared with the chest; proposed wording.

actions.label: Upward rotation of the shoulder blade
actions.plainDescription: Turns the shoulder blade so its socket faces upward, as happens when the arm is raised overhead.
actions.note: Same wording as the shoulders lane's dossier; shared with the shoulders and chest.

actions.label: Downward rotation of the shoulder blade
actions.plainDescription: Turns the shoulder blade so its socket faces downward, as happens when a raised arm is pulled back down to the side.

actions.label: Spine extension
actions.plainDescription: Straightens the trunk from a forward bend, or arches it back.

actions.label: Side bending of the trunk
actions.plainDescription: Bends the trunk to the side.
actions.note: Shared with the core; proposed wording.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Back, Trapezius
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (two searches, Q1 and Q6; generated summaries of the statpearls.com point-of-care copy, 30528, and of the Bookshelf record): a broad, superficial back muscle spanning from the skull and spine out to the shoulder blade; its main job is to move and steady the scapula; the upper fibres elevate and upwardly rotate it, the middle fibres retract it toward the spine, and the lower fibres depress it and help the upper fibres rotate it upward; the scapula's rotation against the levator scapulae and rhomboids, with the deltoid, is essential for throwing; spinal accessory nerve. The Bookshelf id NBK518994 was matched to this title by the search, not opened. Authors and the current update date were not shown (the summary saw copies dated 2023 on statpearls.com and 2026 on the Bookshelf). Section headings were not shown with the excerpts; locators follow StatPearls' usual layout.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Back, Rhomboid Muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (one search, Q7; lines quoted from the Bookshelf copy, the statpearls.com copy 28567 being partly paywalled): 'Functionally, the rhomboid muscles retract, elevate and rotate the scapula. Additionally, the serratus anterior is the antagonist muscle group to the rhomboids.'; they keep the medial border of the scapula in position at the posterior thoracic wall; rhomboid minor from the ligamentum nuchae and C7-T1 to the medial border near the base of the scapular spine; rhomboid major, quadrangular, from T2-T5, inferior to the minor; dorsal scapular nerve and artery; weakness causes winging of the medial border. The direction of the rotation was not stated in the lines seen. Authors not shown; the Bookshelf id was given by the search, not opened.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Thorax, Serratus Anterior Muscles
sources.notes: Seen through the chest lane's searches of 19 Oct 2026 (its Q30 and Q32), not run by this lane: the serratus anterior works with the upper and lower fibres of the trapezius to sustain upward rotation of the scapula, which allows overhead lifting. Expected to be held by the chest lane under this same key; the integration lane keeps one record.

sources.title: StatPearls: back muscles (NBK537216)
sources.notes: Returned by one search on 19 Oct 2026 (Q6) only as a related entry that 'covers the back muscles more broadly and lists the trapezius among the extrinsic back muscles'. Its exact title was not shown, and no excerpt about the erector spinae or the quadratus lumborum was seen; whether it covers the quadratus lumborum is unknown. The draft claims that cite it name it as the reference to check first.

sources.title: Kenhub: trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (two searches, Q1 and Q2; generated summaries that cite this page by result number): the descending fibres work with levator scapulae to elevate the scapula and help hold up the shoulders against gravity when carrying a load; acting on one side they laterally flex the head and neck; the transverse fibres pull the scapula toward the midline and retract it, working with the rhomboids; upward rotation is shared with the serratus anterior; the superior fibres draw the scapula superomedially, the middle fibres medially and the inferior fibres inferomedially. A different Kenhub overview (upper limb muscles and movements) assigned the parts' actions differently and is not cited. Lines are tied to this page by the result number in the summary; Q1 returned it once with a space in the URL ('trapezius muscle').

sources.title: Kenhub: rhomboid muscles
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (one quoted line, Q7): 'Under innervation from the dorsal scapular nerve, the rhomboids primarily retract the scapula superomedially and rotate the glenoid cavity.' The direction of the rotation was not in the line seen.

sources.title: Kenhub: glenohumeral (shoulder) joint
sources.notes: Shared with the shoulders lane (same key and URL). Seen for the back through the chest lane's search of 19 Oct 2026 (its Q56), not run by this lane: 'Adduction is produced by the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major muscles. Together these three are known as the "climbing muscles", as they are powerful adductors.' The search returned three Kenhub pages (this one, the shoulder girdle, and upper limb muscles and movements); tying the line to this page is inferred from the result list, as the shoulders lane did for its flexion line. Extension and internal rotation by these muscles were not in the lines seen.

sources.title: Kenhub: teres minor muscle
sources.notes: Shared with the shoulders lane (same key and URL). Seen for the back only through that lane's recorded excerpt of 19 Oct 2026: the teres major is the teres minor's inferior neighbour ('Teres major lies beneath it').

sources.title: Kenhub: infraspinatus muscle
sources.notes: Shared with the shoulders lane (same key and URL). Seen for the back only through that lane's recorded excerpt of 19 Oct 2026: the infraspinatus 'lies on the dorsal surface of the scapula, deep to trapezius, and parts of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi muscles', so the latissimus dorsi covers part of the back of the shoulder blade.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q4; the page is Elsevier's entry for the left-side model, titled 'Trapezius Muscle (Left)'; the side is dropped from the title so athlete copy carries no screen-side word): describes the whole muscle as elevating, depressing, retracting and upwardly rotating the shoulder girdle, and, contracting on both sides, extending the head and neck.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: descending part of trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q4 and Q5): action 'Elevates, retracts, and upwardly rotates the pectoral girdle at acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints; extends and laterally flexes head and neck'; origin the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line, the nuchal ligament and the C7 spinous process; insertion the posterior aspect of the lateral third of the clavicle and the acromion. Elsevier frames the actions at the joints of the shoulder girdle, not at the scapula alone.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: transverse part of trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q5): origin the spinous processes of C7-T4; insertion the acromion and the lateral end of the spine of the scapula; action 'retracts the pectoral girdle at acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints'; accessory nerve and anterior rami of C3-C4; transverse cervical artery.

sources.title: Elsevier Complete Anatomy, Quick Facts: ascending part of trapezius muscle
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (Q3): origin the spinous processes of T5-T12; insertion the medial end of the spine of the scapula; action 'Depresses, retracts, and upwardly rotates the pectoral (shoulder) girdle at acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints'; accessory nerve and anterior rami of C3-C4; dorsal scapular artery. The same search returned an Elsevier textbook sample chapter (Gray's Anatomy for Students, back) listing 'Elevates scapula (descending part), retracts scapula (transverse part), depresses scapula (ascending part); rotates'; not cited.

deviations.subject: Node actions outside the back's region actions
deviations.finding: §1.2 lists the latissimus dorsi and teres major as external members of the shoulders, whose region actions include shoulder.internal_rotation, and node actions are declared only by a node's home region (§1.3). The back's region actions do not include internal rotation, so as drafted the shoulders page could show these two muscles only under shoulder.extension. Both draft function claims already state that the muscle turns the arm inward.
evidence: No excerpt this session supports internal rotation for either muscle (search budget exhausted); textbook anatomy, to be confirmed.
deviations.proposal: If the follow-up search confirms it and the adversarial review accepts it: add rows (back.latissimus_dorsi, shoulder.internal_rotation, prime) and (back.teres_major, shoulder.internal_rotation, assist) resting on their function claims. The schema has no rule tying a node action to its home region's region actions (node_actions references actions only). Not applied here.

deviations.subject: Neck actions
deviations.finding: The upper trapezius extends the head and neck and bends them to the side (elsevier.trapezius_descending, kenhub.trapezius), and the levator scapulae is described as bending the neck (unconfirmed this session). §1.2 has no neck action; spine.extension and spine.lateral_flexion are worded here for the trunk. The claims state the neck actions as anatomy, and no node action counts them, as the forearm left the hand's actions out.

deviations.subject: back.levator_scapulae layer
deviations.finding: From textbook anatomy, not from an excerpt: part of the levator scapulae lies in the side of the neck between the upper trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid, covered only by fascia and skin. If confirmed, the drawing's Side view could show it as a surface outcrop of an intermediate node. §1.2 is unchanged.

disagreements: Lower trapezius and upward rotation. StatPearls frames the lower fibres mainly as depressors that help the upper fibres rotate the scapula upward; Elsevier lists upward rotation among the ascending part's own actions; StatPearls' serratus anterior article names the upper and lower fibres together. Wording: the lower part 'helps the upper part turn it upward'; node action 'assist'; a caveat says references differ.

Retraction by the upper and lower parts. StatPearls names only the middle fibres as retractors; Elsevier lists retraction for all three parts; Kenhub gives the upper and lower parts' pull a medial component. Wording: 'helps draw the shoulder blade toward the spine'; node actions 'assist'.

Teres major in adduction. Kenhub groups it with the latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major as 'powerful adductors'; Loyola says adduction is 'aided by teres major'. Wording: 'helps bring the arm down'; node action 'prime' (draft), so that the target has a main action; the follow-up should settle it.

A second Kenhub overview (upper limb muscles and movements) assigned elevation and depression to the lower fibres and extension, elevation and retraction to the upper and middle fibres, against Kenhub's own trapezius page, StatPearls and Elsevier. Not cited.

Elsevier frames the trapezius parts' actions at the joints of the shoulder girdle (acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular), StatPearls and Kenhub at the scapula. The claims say 'the shoulder blade', which both framings move.

Summary errors seen: Q7's summary said Wikipedia's rhomboid insertion order 'differs from the StatPearls description', but the StatPearls lines it quoted say the same (major below minor). Q2's line that the ascending fibres are 'effective for depression and upward rotation, with only assistance in retraction' was numbered (5-5), and result 5 in that list was a patent ('Muscle stretching apparatus'); it is not used.

notes.testRuleConflictForIntegration: The forearm test 'gives every muscle a main action' checks every node of kind 'muscle'. back.trapezius is kind 'muscle' with role 'group' and, as a parent, has no node actions (§7.3), so a back test copied from the forearm's would fail on it (the shoulders' deltoid is in the same position). The region test should skip parent nodes.
notes.copyChecks: Every node and claim string was checked by script for the forearm test's patterns: no 'left' or 'right', no per cent sign or 'percent', no 'optimal' or 'guarantee', no 'will grow', no vendor name, no 'table' or 'tables'; cited source titles likewise.
